claim: Schooling in fish is linked to increased foraging success, predator avoidance, and social interactions.
source: Schooling in fish is linked to a number of factors such as increased foraging success, predator avoidance, and social interactions.
evidence: This is a general statement about schooling benefits that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A prevailing hypothesis is that swimming in groups provides energetic benefits through hydrodynamic interactions.
source: In addition, a prevailing hypothesis is that swimming in groups provides energetic benefits through hydrodynamic interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the field, representing established scientific thinking.

claim: Thrust wakes are frequently occurring flow structures in fish schools as they are shed behind swimming fish.
source: Thrust wakes are frequently occurring flow structures in fish schools as they are shed behind swimming fish.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about fish swimming hydrodynamics.

claim: Recent modeling work has suggested that swimming directly in-line behind an individual may lead to increased efficiency despite increased flow speeds in thrust wakes.
source: Despite increased flow speeds in these wakes, recent modeling work has suggested that swimming directly in-line behind an individual may lead to increased efficiency.
evidence: This refers to prior computational/modeling studies in the literature.

claim: Only limited data are available on live fish interacting with thrust wakes.
source: However, only limited data are available on live fish interacting with thrust wakes.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature, representing knowledge of the field.

claim: Brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) swim in thrust wakes generated by a robotic flapping mechanism.
source: We show that trout swim in thrust wakes, reduce their tail-beat frequencies, and synchronize with the robotic flapping mechanism.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Brook trout reduce their tail-beat frequencies when swimming in thrust wakes.
source: We show that trout swim in thrust wakes, reduce their tail-beat frequencies, and synchronize with the robotic flapping mechanism.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by kinematic measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Brook trout synchronize with the robotic flapping mechanism when swimming in thrust wakes.
source: We show that trout swim in thrust wakes, reduce their tail-beat frequencies, and synchronize with the robotic flapping mechanism.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data showing frequency matching and phase relationships (Figures 3, 4).

claim: Trout interact with oncoming vortices when swimming in thrust wakes.
source: Our flow and pressure field analysis revealed that the trout are interacting with oncoming vortices and that they exhibit reduced pressure drag at the head compared to swimming in isolation.
evidence: This is supported by PIV flow visualization data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Trout exhibit reduced pressure drag at the head compared to swimming in isolation when in thrust wakes.
source: Our flow and pressure field analysis revealed that the trout are interacting with oncoming vortices and that they exhibit reduced pressure drag at the head compared to swimming in isolation.
evidence: This is supported by computational pressure field analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Trout swim energetically more efficiently in thrust wakes.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that trout swim energetically more efficiently in thrust wakes and support the hypothesis that swimming in the wake of one another is an advantageous strategy to save energy in a school.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence: reduced tail-beat frequency, reduced pressure drag, and synchronization behavior.

claim: Swimming in the wake of one another is an advantageous strategy to save energy in a school.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that trout swim energetically more efficiently in thrust wakes and support the hypothesis that swimming in the wake of one another is an advantageous strategy to save energy in a school.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental findings on reduced tail-beat frequency and pressure drag.

claim: Schooling fish exhibit reduced tail-beat frequencies relative to solitary individuals.
source: Recent work supports this hypothesis on the basis of experiments where schooling fish exhibit reduced tail-beat frequencies relative to solitary individuals which suggests decreased energy consumption by the group as a whole (Ashraf et al., 2017; Marras et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Reduced tail-beat frequencies in schooling fish suggest decreased energy consumption by the group as a whole.
source: Recent work supports this hypothesis on the basis of experiments where schooling fish exhibit reduced tail-beat frequencies relative to solitary individuals which suggests decreased energy consumption by the group as a whole (Ashraf et al., 2017; Marras et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between tail-beat frequency and metabolic cost, supported by citations.

claim: Fish swimming side-by-side in phalanx formation benefit from the channeling/wall effect.
source: The phalanx or soldier formation describes fish swimming side-by-side, parallel to each other (Figure 1A), and fish in this position are expected to benefit from the channeling/wall effect and simulation studies Daghooghi and Borazjani, 2015; Hemelrijk et al., 2015 have shown increased efficiency for this formation.
evidence: This is supported by simulation studies cited in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Simulation studies have shown increased efficiency for phalanx formation in fish.
source: The phalanx or soldier formation describes fish swimming side-by-side, parallel to each other (Figure 1A), and fish in this position are expected to benefit from the channeling/wall effect and simulation studies Daghooghi and Borazjani, 2015; Hemelrijk et al., 2015 have shown increased efficiency for this formation.
evidence: This is directly supported by citations to simulation studies.

claim: Phalanx formation is linked to reduced energy consumption in red nose tetras swimming in a school.
source: And Ashraf et al., 2017 linked the phalanx formation to reduced energy consumption in red nose tetras swimming in a school.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Leading swimmers experience increased thrust due to additional effective added mass at the tail trailing edge caused by blockage of water by trailing swimmers.
source: Here, the leading swimmer is thought to experience increased thrust because of the additional effective added mass at the tail trailing edge due to blockage of water by the trailing swimmer behind.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on fluid dynamics principles.

claim: Simulations on pitching foils have confirmed increased thrust for leading swimmers due to trailing swimmer blockage effects.
source: Simulations on pitching foils Bao and Tao, 2014; Saadat et al., 2021 have confirmed this effect and show increased overall hydrodynamic efficiency for the two-body system of leading and trailing swimmers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to simulation studies.

claim: Fish swimming at the front of schools of gray mullet show reduced tail-beat frequencies compared to swimming in isolation.
source: Measurements of reduced tail-beat frequencies of fish swimming at the front of schools of gray mullet compared to swimming in isolation further support these findings (Marras et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental measurements.

claim: Fish thrust wakes are characterized by a vortex street of alternating orientation and increased average flow speed compared to the free stream.
source: Fish thrust wakes are characterized by both a vortex street of alternating orientation, and an increased average flow speed compared to the free stream (Blickhan et al., 1992; Müller et al., 1997; Nauen and Lauder, 2002; Tytell, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Weihs hypothesized that fish directly behind another would experience higher relative velocity and would have to exert extra energy.
source: Weihs hypothesized that fish directly behind another would experience a higher relative velocity and would have to exert extra energy and suggested that the most efficient swimming position lies midway between two preceding fish (Figure 1C) resulting in a diamond formation.
evidence: This is a historical hypothesis from the literature, cited implicitly through reference to Weihs.

claim: Weihs suggested that the most efficient swimming position lies midway between two preceding fish, resulting in a diamond formation.
source: Weihs hypothesized that fish directly behind another would experience a higher relative velocity and would have to exert extra energy and suggested that the most efficient swimming position lies midway between two preceding fish (Figure 1C) resulting in a diamond formation.
evidence: This is a historical hypothesis from the literature, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Fish swimming in diamond formation encounter flow conditions resembling a von Kármán drag wake.
source: A fish swimming in this diamond formation encounters flow conditions resembling a von Kármán drag wake, similar to the one shed by a cylinder under sufficiently high flow speeds.
evidence: This is an inference based on fluid dynamics principles and the geometry of the diamond formation.

claim: Trout show reduced muscle activity when swimming in a drag wake.
source: Liao et al., 2003 explored this scenario in trout and found reduced muscle activity for fish swimming in a drag wake, and direct measurements of energy consumption confirm that fish experience reduced energetic costs when in a drag wake (Taguchi and Liao, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Fish experience reduced energetic costs when swimming in a drag wake.
source: Liao et al., 2003 explored this scenario in trout and found reduced muscle activity for fish swimming in a drag wake, and direct measurements of energy consumption confirm that fish experience reduced energetic costs when in a drag wake (Taguchi and Liao, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to direct measurements of energy consumption.

claim: Recent work suggests that swimming in tandem provides hydrodynamic advantages.
source: In contrast to Weihs' argument that in-line fish positions are disadvantageous (Figure 1D), some recent work suggests that swimming in tandem provides hydrodynamic advantages.
evidence: This is supported by references to recent simulations and experiments cited in the following sentence.

claim: Simulations, flapping foil experiments, and robot experiments indicate increased thrust production and efficiency when a fish or flapping foil swims in a thrust wake.
source: Simulations (Hemelrijk et al., 2015; Maertens et al., 2017), flapping foil experiments (Boschitsch et al., 2014; Kurt and Moored, 2018), and robot experiments (Saadat et al., 2021) indicate increased thrust production and efficiency when a fish or flapping foil swims in a thrust wake.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to simulations and experiments.

claim: A swimmer in a thrust wake experiences oncoming flow at its leading-edge with an oscillating angle of attack and is subject to lift forces that have components in forward direction.
source: The fluid dynamic benefits to the follower occur because the swimmer in the thrust wake experiences the oncoming flow at its leading-edge with an oscillating angle of attack and is subject to lift forces that have components in forward direction.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on fluid dynamics principles.

claim: A downstream swimmer can reduce its drag by turning its head in a manner that employs the oncoming vortex flow to increase the transverse velocity across the head.
source: Maertens et. al (Maertens et al., 2017) argue that a downstream swimmer can reduce its drag by consistently turning its head in a manner that employs the oncoming vortex flow to increase the transverse velocity across the head.
evidence: This is an argument from a cited simulation study.

claim: Pressure drag at the head can be decreased substantially when swimming in a thrust wake, resulting in increased efficiency.
source: As a result, the pressure drag at the head can be decreased substantially and result in increased efficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism described by Maertens et al.

claim: Experimental data on live fish exploiting thrust wake conditions is lacking.
source: Although recent modeling work suggests advantages for in-line swimming, experimental data on live fish exploiting these conditions is lacking.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature.

claim: Brook trout swim against oncoming currents in their natural habitat.
source: We chose trout (brook trout, Salvelinus fontinalis) for our investigation as this species swims against oncoming currents in their natural habitat and is known to sense and take advantage of flow structures that can reduce energy use (McLaughlin and Noakes, 1998; Shuler et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge about trout behavior supported by citations.

claim: Brook trout are known to sense and take advantage of flow structures that can reduce energy use.
source: We chose trout (brook trout, Salvelinus fontinalis) for our investigation as this species swims against oncoming currents in their natural habitat and is known to sense and take advantage of flow structures that can reduce energy use (McLaughlin and Noakes, 1998; Shuler et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Fish moving in fluids use vision, the lateral line, and the vestibular system to control their body motion.
source: Fish moving in fluids use (1) vision, (2) the lateral line, and (3) the vestibular system to control their body motion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fish sensory systems.

claim: Vision, lateral line, and vestibular system in fish have been the subject of numerous studies.
source: All of them have been the subject of numerous studies over the years (Ali, 2013; Coombs and Montgomery, 2014; Platt, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review or foundational studies.

claim: The individuals in the experiments had vision, lateral line, and vestibular system sensor modalities available.
source: The individuals in our experiments had all of these sensor modalities available.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions.

claim: The flapping foil generates accelerated flows with similar hydrodynamic characteristics to those of live fish in terms of Strouhal number and relative axial and lateral spacing of shed vortices.
source: Using a flapping foil allowed us to generate accelerated flows with similar hydrodynamic characteristics, in terms of the Strouhal number and the relative axial and lateral spacing of shed vortices, to those of live fish (Anderson et al., 1998; Buchholz and Smits, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on flapping foils and comparison to fish swimming.

claim: The robotic flapping motion generates fish-like thrust wakes.
source: By carefully choosing the robotic flapping motion, we generated fish-like thrust wakes and introduced trout to these conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and flow visualization data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Trout swim in-line with the flapping foil.
source: We found that trout swim in-line with the flapping foil (Videos 1 and 2) and reduce their tail-beat frequencies compared to swimming at the same effective flow speeds under free-stream conditions.
evidence: This is supported by video evidence and experimental observations.

claim: Trout reduce their tail-beat frequencies compared to swimming at the same effective flow speeds under free-stream conditions when swimming in thrust wakes.
source: We found that trout swim in-line with the flapping foil (Videos 1 and 2) and reduce their tail-beat frequencies compared to swimming at the same effective flow speeds under free-stream conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by kinematic data in Figure 3A.

claim: Particle image velocimetry revealed that individuals interact directly with oncoming thrust wake vortices.
source: Further analyses employing particle image velocimetry revealed that individuals interact directly with oncoming thrust wake vortices.
evidence: This is supported by PIV flow visualization data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Pressure field computations showed reduced average pressures at the leading-edge of trout swimming in thrust wakes, suggesting reduced pressure drag.
source: Finally, our pressure field computations showed reduced average pressures at the leading-edge suggesting reduced pressure drag and reduced swimming costs.
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis of pressure fields shown in Figure 6.

claim: Reduced average pressures at the leading-edge suggest reduced swimming costs for trout in thrust wakes.
source: Finally, our pressure field computations showed reduced average pressures at the leading-edge suggesting reduced pressure drag and reduced swimming costs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between pressure drag and swimming cost.

claim: The findings support the hypothesis that fish can reduce swimming costs under in-line swimming conditions.
source: These findings support the hypothesis that fish can reduce swimming costs under in-line swimming conditions and help explain why in-line swimming is common in schools of fish.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The findings help explain why in-line swimming is common in schools of fish.
source: These findings support the hypothesis that fish can reduce swimming costs under in-line swimming conditions and help explain why in-line swimming is common in schools of fish.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to observed behavior in nature.

claim: The thrust wake generated by the flapping foil is characterized by a reverse Kármán vortex street and increased flow speeds in the wake.
source: The thrust wake generated by the flapping foil is characterized by a reverse Kármán vortex street and increased flow speeds in the wake (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) comparable to the wakes generated by swimming trout (Nauen and Lauder, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by flow visualization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The thrust wake generated by the flapping foil is comparable to the wakes generated by swimming trout.
source: The thrust wake generated by the flapping foil is characterized by a reverse Kármán vortex street and increased flow speeds in the wake (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) comparable to the wakes generated by swimming trout (Nauen and Lauder, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited prior work and flow visualization data.

claim: Matching the Strouhal number of swimming fish and the flapping foil ensures similar hydrodynamics in terms of the relative axial and lateral spacing between vortices.
source: Matching the Strouhal number of swimming fish and our flapping foil ensures similar hydrodynamics in terms of the relative axial and lateral spacing between vortices.
evidence: This is based on fluid dynamics principles relating Strouhal number to wake structure.

claim: The relatively large span of the flapping foil induces thrust wakes along a larger depth and increases the chance that fish encounter the wake in the flow tank.
source: It is worth noting that the relatively large span of the flapping foil induces thrust wakes along a larger depth and thus increases the chance that fish encounter the wake in the flow tank, however at the expense of producing two-dimensional (planar) thrust wakes.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental design and its consequences.

claim: The large span of the flapping foil produces two-dimensional (planar) thrust wakes.
source: It is worth noting that the relatively large span of the flapping foil induces thrust wakes along a larger depth and thus increases the chance that fish encounter the wake in the flow tank, however at the expense of producing two-dimensional (planar) thrust wakes.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the wake produced by the experimental apparatus.

claim: Smaller fish showed a decrease of 28.3% in mean tail-beat frequency when exposed to thrust wakes.
source: Smaller fish showed a decrease of 28.3%, and larger fish showed a decrease of 14.7% in the mean frequency.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from kinematic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Larger fish showed a decrease of 14.7% in mean tail-beat frequency when exposed to thrust wakes.
source: Smaller fish showed a decrease of 28.3%, and larger fish showed a decrease of 14.7% in the mean frequency.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from kinematic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fish maintained their position in the thrust wake by beating their tails less often than when they swam at the same ground speed in free-stream flow.
source: This suggests that fish maintained their position in the thrust wake by beating their tails less often than when they swam at the same ground speed in free-stream flow.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed reduction in tail-beat frequency.

claim: For both smaller (mean ± s.d.: 2.15 ± 0.29 Hz) and larger (1.96 ± 0.04 Hz) fish, the swimming frequency approached the 2 Hz flapping foil motion when swimming in the foil thrust wake.
source: For both smaller (mean ± s.d.: 2.15 ± 0.29 Hz) and larger (1.96 ± 0.04 Hz) fish the swimming frequency approached the 2 Hz flapping foil motion when swimming in the foil thrust wake.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from kinematic analysis demonstrating frequency synchronization.

claim: Fish swimming in the thrust wake showed decreased overall phase lags along the body in both size groups compared to the free stream control condition.
source: We analyzed body bending kinematics and identified decreased overall phase lags along the body in the thrust wake in both size groups (Figure 3B) compared to the free stream control condition.
evidence: This is a result from kinematic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Decreased overall phase lags relate to the bending of consecutive body segments being timed closer together.
source: As a result, the bending of consecutive body segments was timed closer together (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phase lag data illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: Smaller overall phase lags relate to fewer waves along the body.
source: Smaller overall phase lags also relate to fewer waves along the body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between phase lag and body wave number.

claim: There were no significant differences in body amplitude between fish that swam in thrust wakes and in the free stream.
source: We did not find any significant differences in body amplitude between fish that swam in thrust wakes and in the free stream (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from kinematic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fish time their body undulations and tail-beats depending on their location in the thrust wake.
source: This result demonstrates that fish time their body undulations and tail-beats depending on their location in the thrust wake, and it suggests that they synchronize their movements to the oncoming vortices that are shed by the flapping foil.
evidence: This is an inference from the linear relationship between phase difference and distance.

claim: Fish synchronize their movements to the oncoming vortices that are shed by the flapping foil.
source: This result demonstrates that fish time their body undulations and tail-beats depending on their location in the thrust wake, and it suggests that they synchronize their movements to the oncoming vortices that are shed by the flapping foil.
evidence: This is an inference from the phase-distance relationship and vortex interaction observations.

claim: Trout in thrust wakes interact with oncoming vortices that are shed from the flapping foil and time their movements accordingly.
source: Analysis of flapper wake velocity fields show that trout in the thrust wakes interact with oncoming vortices that are shed from the flapping foil and time their movements accordingly.
evidence: This is supported by PIV analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Two scenarios of vortex interaction were identified: double-sided and single-sided vortex interaction.
source: We identified two scenarios that we call double-sided and single-sided vortex interaction.
evidence: This is a classification based on PIV observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Double-sided vortex interaction is characterized by an initial vortex interception which splits the vortex in two parts.
source: Double-sided vortex interaction (Figure 5A–F, Video 5) is characterized by an initial vortex interception which splits the vortex in two parts.
evidence: This is a description of observed flow patterns shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: In double-sided vortex interaction, one part of the vortex stays attached and 'rolls' downstream along the body, whereas the other part is shed laterally and moves away from the body.
source: One part of the vortex stays attached and 'rolls'' downstream along the body, whereas the other part is shed laterally and moves away from the body.
evidence: This is a description of observed flow patterns in PIV data.

claim: In double-sided vortex interaction, the trout body alternates between clockwise and counter-clockwise vortices that are intercepted, stay attached and roll along corresponding alternate sides of the body.
source: In this situation, the trout body alternates between clockwise and counter-clockwise vortices that are intercepted, stay attached and roll along corresponding alternate sides of the body.
evidence: This is a description of observed flow patterns in PIV data.

claim: Fish are able to 'catch' vortices on both sides of the body in double-sided vortex interaction.
source: Fish are thus able to 'catch vortices on both sides of the body.
evidence: This is a summary description of the double-sided vortex interaction pattern.

claim: Single-sided vortex interactions occur for only one of the two differently oriented vortex types that are shed from the foil.
source: Single-sided vortex interactions (Figure 5G–L) undergo the same process of 'catching vortices'; however, only for one of the two differently oriented vortex types that are shed from the foil.
evidence: This is a description of observed flow patterns shown in Figure 5G-L.

claim: In single-sided vortex interactions, the intercepted vortex stays attached and 'rolls' only along one side of the body.
source: Consequently, the intercepted vortex stays attached and 'rolls' only along one side of the body.
evidence: This is a description of observed flow patterns in PIV data.

claim: Single-sided vortex interactions are related to a slight lateral offset of fish position with respect to the center line around which the foil is oscillating.
source: The single-sided vortex interactions are related to a slight lateral offset of fish position with respect to the center line around which the foil is oscillating, whereas double-sided vortex interactions occur for fish swimming directly in the center line.
evidence: This is an observation about the relationship between fish position and vortex interaction type.

claim: Double-sided vortex interactions occur for fish swimming directly in the center line of foil oscillation.
source: The single-sided vortex interactions are related to a slight lateral offset of fish position with respect to the center line around which the foil is oscillating, whereas double-sided vortex interactions occur for fish swimming directly in the center line.
evidence: This is an observation about the relationship between fish position and vortex interaction type.

claim: Vortex interactions occurred at different distances with respect to the foil.
source: We also note that vortex interactions occurred at different distances with respect to the foil (d1 and d2 in Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from PIV data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The consistent interaction pattern between the trout body and oncoming vortices indicates that fish are synchronizing their movements with respect to the flapping foil and the corresponding vortices shed into the wake.
source: The consistent interaction pattern between the trout body and oncoming vortices indicates that these fish are synchronizing their movements with respect to the flapping foil and the corresponding vortices shed into the wake.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed vortex interaction patterns.

claim: A large part of the drag on a swimming fish at Reynolds numbers greater than 5000 is caused by drag forces at the anterior portion of the body that faces the oncoming flow.
source: A large part of the drag on a swimming fish at Reynolds numbers greater than 5000 is caused by drag forces at the anterior portion of the body that faces the oncoming flow (Du Clos et al., 2019; Lucas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The computed pressure fields revealed reduced average head pressures in the thrust wake compared to free-stream swimming.
source: The computed pressure fields revealed reduced average head pressures in the thrust wake (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from computational pressure field analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The strongest decreases in head pressure (46% and 86% decrease compared to free-stream swimming) were found for fish swimming close to the foil and exploiting double-sided vortex interactions.
source: We found the strongest decreases (46% and 86% decrease compared to free-stream swimming) for fish swimming close to the foil and exploiting double-sided vortex interactions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pressure field analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Fish swimming further away from the foil and exhibiting single-sided vortex interactions showed reduced average head pressure magnitudes (45% decrease) compared to free-stream swimming.
source: Fish swimming further away from the foil and exhibiting single-sided vortex interactions also showed reduced average head pressure magnitudes compared to free-stream swimming (45% decrease).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pressure field analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fish exhibiting single-sided vortex interactions showed an asymmetric average pressure pattern with higher average pressures at the side closer to the centerline of the foil oscillation.
source: Here, we found an asymmetric average pressure pattern with higher average pressures at the side closer to the centerline of the foil oscillation.
evidence: This is an observation from pressure field analysis.

claim: The flapping foil induces oscillating negative and positive pressure zones around the head.
source: Here, it becomes evident that the flapping foil induces oscillating negative and positive pressure zones around the head.
evidence: This is an observation from instantaneous pressure field analysis shown in Figure 6D1-D4.

claim: Negative pressure (suction) zones cause forward thrust forces, whereas positive pressures contribute to drag.
source: The negative pressure (suction) zones cause forward thrust forces, whereas the positive pressures contribute to drag.
evidence: This is based on fluid dynamics principles relating pressure to force direction.

claim: On average, oscillating pressures reduce overall head drag because positive pressure magnitudes are comparable to free-stream swimming but mean head pressure is reduced by the occurrence of negative head pressures for part of the cycle.
source: On average, this reduces overall head drag as the positive pressure magnitudes are comparable to free-stream swimming but mean head pressure is reduced by the occurrence of negative head pressures for part of the cycle.
evidence: This is an inference from the instantaneous and average pressure field data.

claim: The pressure analysis indicates that the drag of fish swimming in thrust wakes is reduced compared to free-stream swimming.
source: This pressure analysis indicates that the drag of fish swimming in thrust wakes is reduced compared to free-stream swimming, and therefore supports the hypothesis of decreased energy used to hold station in thrust wakes with accelerated mean flow.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the pressure field analysis.

claim: The pressure analysis supports the hypothesis of decreased energy used to hold station in thrust wakes with accelerated mean flow.
source: This pressure analysis indicates that the drag of fish swimming in thrust wakes is reduced compared to free-stream swimming, and therefore supports the hypothesis of decreased energy used to hold station in thrust wakes with accelerated mean flow.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the pressure field analysis.

claim: Fish in schools often assume an in-line configuration with one fish swimming directly behind another.
source: But fish in schools often assume an in-line configuration with one fish swimming directly behind another (Video 6).
evidence: This is an observation of natural fish schooling behavior, supported by video evidence.

claim: Some authors suggest that swimming in tandem is not an energetically favorable configuration due to the accelerated wake flows generated by the fish in front.
source: Some authors (Verma et al., 2018; Weihs, 1973) suggest that swimming in tandem is not an energetically favorable configuration due to the accelerated wake flows generated by the fish in front.
evidence: This is a summary of arguments from cited literature.

claim: Primarily computational studies have suggested that a trailing streamlined shape could experience reduced energetic cost due to leading edge suction resulting from oscillating flow impinging on the head or leading edge.
source: Other, primarily computational studies have suggested that a trailing streamlined shape could in fact experience reduced energetic cost due to leading edge suction resulting from an oscillating flow impinging on the head or leading edge of the trailing fish or foil (Kurt and Moored, 2018; Maertens et al., 2017; Saadat et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited computational studies.

claim: No experimental study prior to this work has demonstrated that live fish will voluntarily swim in a thrust wake and that reduced swimming cost could result from such a position.
source: To date, however, no experimental study has demonstrated that live fish will voluntarily swim in a thrust wake and that reduced swimming cost could result from such a position.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature prior to this study.

claim: This study documents that trout perform volitional in-line swimming with their body located within the accelerated flow region.
source: With these experiments, we document that trout indeed perform volitional in-line swimming with their body located within the accelerated flow region, and our analysis suggests that they can save energy under these conditions.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental observations.

claim: The analysis suggests that trout can save energy when swimming in-line in thrust wakes.
source: With these experiments, we document that trout indeed perform volitional in-line swimming with their body located within the accelerated flow region, and our analysis suggests that they can save energy under these conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including reduced tail-beat frequency and reduced pressure drag.

claim: A drag wake in the context of fish swimming is characterized by a von Kármán vortex street between two thrust wakes.
source: A drag wake in the context of fish swimming and schooling is characterized by a von Kármán vortex street between two thrust wakes (e.g., shed by two fish swimming parallel to each other).
evidence: This is a definition based on fluid dynamics knowledge.

claim: The average flow speed in a drag wake is inherently slower than in the free stream.
source: It is important to note that the average flow speed in a drag wake is inherently slower than in the free stream.
evidence: This is based on fluid dynamics principles of drag wakes.

claim: A dead fish can propel itself forward in the wake of a cylinder.
source: This is highlighted in experiments that demonstrate a dead fish propelling itself forward in the wake of a cylinder (Beal et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Trailing cyclists benefit from reduced relative oncoming flow which results in reduced aerodynamic drag when drafting.
source: This situation is an example of a drag wake and the reduced costs that ensue from moving in that reduced velocity zone: trailing cyclists benefit from the reduced relative oncoming flow which results in reduced aerodynamic drag.
evidence: This is an analogy based on general knowledge of aerodynamics.

claim: Vortex orientations in thrust wakes are reversed compared to drag wakes (termed a reverse Kármán vortex street).
source: Vortex orientations are reversed compared to the drag wake (termed a reverse Kármán vortex street), and, notably, thrust wakes are characterized by a higher average flow speed than in the free stream.
evidence: This is established knowledge about thrust wake characteristics.

claim: Thrust wakes are characterized by a higher average flow speed than in the free stream.
source: Vortex orientations are reversed compared to the drag wake (termed a reverse Kármán vortex street), and, notably, thrust wakes are characterized by a higher average flow speed than in the free stream.
evidence: This is established knowledge about thrust wake characteristics.

claim: For swimming fish, increased flow speed in thrust wakes is a consequence of tail fin movement which actively generates thrust.
source: For swimming fish, this is a consequence of tail fin movement which actively generates thrust so that individual fish located behind this thrust wake experiences higher than free stream mean flow velocities.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the mechanics of fish swimming.

claim: Individual fish located behind a thrust wake experience higher than free stream mean flow velocities.
source: For swimming fish, this is a consequence of tail fin movement which actively generates thrust so that individual fish located behind this thrust wake experiences higher than free stream mean flow velocities.
evidence: This is a consequence of thrust wake characteristics.

claim: A key difference between thrust wakes and drag wakes is the undulatory characteristic of thrust wakes produced by swimming fish.
source: A key difference is the undulatory characteristic of thrust wakes that are produced by swimming fish.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of fish swimming hydrodynamics.

claim: A trailing fish faces the oncoming flow at its head with an oscillating angle of attack.
source: A trailing fish faces the oncoming flow at its head with an oscillating angle of attack, and (unlike the trailing cyclist) the trailing fish oscillates its head during swimming (Di Santo et al., 2021) further enhancing the time-dependent variation in flow in the head region.
evidence: This is based on the nature of thrust wakes and fish swimming kinematics, supported by citation.

claim: The trailing fish oscillates its head during swimming, further enhancing the time-dependent variation in flow in the head region.
source: A trailing fish faces the oncoming flow at its head with an oscillating angle of attack, and (unlike the trailing cyclist) the trailing fish oscillates its head during swimming (Di Santo et al., 2021) further enhancing the time-dependent variation in flow in the head region.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on fish head oscillation.

claim: As a result of the oscillatory wake impinging on the fish head, the pressure distribution in the head region is composed of both positive and negative pressures, effectively reducing overall pressure drag.
source: Our analysis showed that as a result of the oscillatory wake impinging on the fish head the pressure distribution in the head region is composed of both positive and negative pressures, and thus effectively reduces the overall pressure drag.
evidence: This is a finding from the pressure field analysis in this study.

claim: The finding that oscillatory wakes reduce pressure drag is in agreement with previous simulation analyses.
source: This is in agreement with previous simulation analyses (Maertens et al., 2017; Saadat et al., 2021) and makes in-line swimming an advantageous formation for fish.
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior computational work.

claim: The findings make in-line swimming an advantageous formation for fish.
source: This is in agreement with previous simulation analyses (Maertens et al., 2017; Saadat et al., 2021) and makes in-line swimming an advantageous formation for fish.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Fish in thrust wakes are exhibiting vortex phase matching.
source: Together with our PIV analysis, these results suggest that trout are exhibiting vortex phase matching (Li et al., 2020) which has been identified as an energy saving mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the synchronization behavior and vortex interaction patterns, with reference to prior work.

claim: Vortex phase matching has been identified as an energy saving mechanism.
source: Together with our PIV analysis, these results suggest that trout are exhibiting vortex phase matching (Li et al., 2020) which has been identified as an energy saving mechanism.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Lower tail-beat frequencies without significant changes in amplitude are reflective of reduced metabolic cost.
source: Apart from the reduced hydrodynamic resistance, the lower tail-beat frequencies without significant changes in amplitude also are reflective of reduced metabolic cost (Ohlberger et al., 2007; Steinhausen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The change in phase lags suggests a change in the muscle activation pattern along the body.
source: The change in phase lags that we observed further suggests a change in the muscle activation pattern along the body.
evidence: This is an inference from the kinematic observations.

claim: Decreased muscle activation was observed when trout swim with a Karman gait in a drag wake.
source: Decreased muscle activation was observed by Liao et al., 2003 when trout swim with a Karman gait in a drag wake, and passive dynamics could therefore be additional sources for energy savings that would however need to be confirmed in future experiments.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Passive dynamics could be additional sources for energy savings in thrust wake swimming but need to be confirmed in future experiments.
source: Decreased muscle activation was observed by Liao et al., 2003 when trout swim with a Karman gait in a drag wake, and passive dynamics could therefore be additional sources for energy savings that would however need to be confirmed in future experiments.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms that requires future investigation.

claim: The data suggests that fish can swim more efficiently in thrust wakes because they maintain the same swimming speed as in the free stream while facing reduced pressure drag and spending less energy by beating their tail less frequently.
source: Overall, our data suggests that fish can swim more efficiently in thrust wakes because they maintain the same swimming speed as in the free stream while facing reduced pressure drag and spending less energy by beating their tail less frequently.
evidence: This is a synthesis of multiple experimental findings.

claim: The results are in agreement with past simulation and robot studies.
source: These results are in agreement with past simulation and robot studies.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work in the literature.

claim: Harvey et al. exposed rainbow trout to a hydrofoil thrust wake and observed altered swimming gaits and estimated energy savings via measurements of acceleration.
source: (Harvey et al., 2022) adopted a similar approach to ours and exposed rainbow trout to a hydrofoil thrust wake. They also observed altered swimming gaits and estimated energy savings but via measurements of acceleration.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Harvey et al. used juvenile trout about three times smaller than trout used in this study, but at similar foil cord length.
source: It should also be noted that they used juveniles about three times smaller than trout used in our study, however at similar foil cord length.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental conditions between studies.

claim: Fish in thrust wakes may exhibit energetic benefits over an extended size scale.
source: This indicates that fish in thrust wakes may exhibit energetic benefits over an extended size scale.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison with Harvey et al.'s work.

claim: Verma et al. explored simulated leader-follower formations in a reinforcement learning framework.
source: (Verma et al., 2018) explored simulated leader-follower formations in a reinforcement learning framework.
evidence: This is a summary of a cited computational study.

claim: In Verma et al.'s first set of optimizations with a reward function based on modified Froude efficiency, followers settled close to the center line of the leader's wake and showed well-coordinated behavior.
source: A first set of optimizations with a reward function based on a modified Froude efficiency led to formations in which followers settled close to the center line of the leader's wake and showed well-coordinated behavior of the follower with the wake.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited simulation study.

claim: Verma et al. concluded that swimming in-line with a leader is not associated with energetic benefits for the follower based on simulations where the follower strictly tries to attain an in-line position regardless of energetic considerations.
source: In the same work, Verma et al., 2018 concluded in a second set of simulations that swimming in-line with a leader is not associated with energetic benefits for the follower. It is important to note that this conclusion was drawn based on a swimming strategy in which the follower would strictly try to attain an in-line position regardless of energetic considerations.
evidence: This is a summary and interpretation of findings from a cited study.

claim: In Verma et al.'s simulations, the optimization led to increased swimming amplitude, which permitted in-line swimming but at a higher energetic cost.
source: As a consequence, the optimization led to an increased swimming amplitude, which permitted in-line swimming but at a higher energetic cost.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited simulation study.

claim: In-line swimming by itself is not necessarily energetically beneficial.
source: We confirm that in-line swimming by itself is not necessarily energetically beneficial.
evidence: This is a conclusion that agrees with aspects of prior work.

claim: Efficient swimming requires the correct timing of interactions with the wake.
source: More importantly, efficient swimming requires the correct timing of interactions with the wake.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings on synchronization and vortex interactions.

claim: In-line positions are favorable conditions to maintain wake synchronization as found in experiments of double-sided vortex interactions.
source: Rather than viewing in-line swimming as a policy, we can see in-line positions as favorable conditions to maintain wake synchronization as we found in our experiments of double-sided vortex interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: In-line swimming has been dismissed as a beneficial strategy considering the diverging characteristics of three-dimensional versus two-dimensional wakes.
source: Finally, in-line swimming has been dismissed as a beneficial strategy in the past considering the diverging characteristics of three-dimensional compared versus two-dimensional wakes (Verma et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of arguments from cited literature.

claim: It could be argued that in diverging wakes, the area around the centerline is composed of quiescent flow and in-line swimming offers no opportunity to interact with vortices.
source: In such cases, it could be argued that the area around the centerline of the wake is composed of quiescent flow and in-line swimming offers no opportunity to interact with vortices.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about wake structure.

claim: Diverging wakes are predominantly found in simulation studies at lower Reynolds numbers.
source: Whereas these diverging wakes are predominantly found in simulation studies at lower Reynolds numbers (Borazjani and Sotiropoulos, 2008; Liu and Dong, 2016; Verma et al., 2018), we found no evidence for bifurcating wake structures behind trout swimming in the free stream, a finding in line with previous analyses of trout wake flow patterns (Müller et al., 1997; Tytell, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to simulation studies and comparison to experimental observations.

claim: No evidence was found for bifurcating wake structures behind trout swimming in the free stream.
source: Whereas these diverging wakes are predominantly found in simulation studies at lower Reynolds numbers (Borazjani and Sotiropoulos, 2008; Liu and Dong, 2016; Verma et al., 2018), we found no evidence for bifurcating wake structures behind trout swimming in the free stream, a finding in line with previous analyses of trout wake flow patterns (Müller et al., 1997; Tytell, 2010).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, consistent with prior work.

claim: The artificial thrust wake generated using the robotic flapping foil produced a parallel vortex street similar to observations of the wake in freely swimming trout.
source: The artificial thrust wake generated using our robotic flapping foil produced a parallel vortex street similar to our observations of the wake in freely swimming trout.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental observations between the robotic wake and fish wake.

claim: Energy-efficient thrust wake interactions could occur in diverging wakes with a small offset to the centerline.
source: In addition, given the experimental data on single-sided vortex interactions, we hypothesize that energy-efficient thrust wake interactions could also occur in diverging wakes but with a small offset to the centerline.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the single-sided vortex interaction observations.

claim: The 3D kinematics of the tail are determined by the 3D body shape as well as the motion.
source: The 3D kinematics of the tail are determined by the 3D body shape as well as the motion (Tytell et al., 2008), and it has been shown that the tips of the caudal fin are subject to cupping into the flow.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The tips of the caudal fin are subject to cupping into the flow.
source: The 3D kinematics of the tail are determined by the 3D body shape as well as the motion (Tytell et al., 2008), and it has been shown that the tips of the caudal fin are subject to cupping into the flow.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fish tail kinematics.

claim: The flapping foil in this study is rigid and does not exactly replicate the cupping motion pattern of fish tails.
source: The flapping foil in our study is rigid and does therefore not exactly replicate this motion pattern.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the experimental apparatus.

claim: Future work could address the gap in replicating tail flexibility by using a flexible flapping foil.
source: Future work could address this gap by using a flexible flapping foil.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: 3D vortex rings shed at the caudal fin induce flow in lateral (side-to-side), axial (forward-backward), and vertical (up-down) swimming directions.
source: Another aspect of 3D fish swimming are 3D vortex rings that are shed into the thrust wake at the caudal fin. These structures induce flow in (1) lateral (side-to-side) and axial (forward-backward) swimming directions as well as in (2) the vertical (up-down) swimming direction.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of 3D fish swimming hydrodynamics.

claim: Lateral and axial flow components are important for thrust generation to swim forward.
source: These flow components are arguably important for thrust generation to swim forward and we showed in our study how fish interact with these flows and benefit from reduced pressure drag.
evidence: This is based on understanding of swimming mechanics.

claim: Vertical flow components need to be included in future experiments to address how up-and-down flow dynamics impact fish in a thrust wake.
source: Vertical components need to be included in future experiments to address how the up-and-down flow dynamics impact fish in a thrust wake.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research to address a limitation.

claim: The results are likely to extrapolate to 3D fish swimming despite the 2D nature of the experimental wake.
source: Nonetheless, our results contribute to a better understanding of in-line swimming in thrust wakes and are likely to extrapolate to 3D fish swimming.
evidence: This is speculation about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: A limited number (n = 3) of swimming trials were analyzed using PIV.
source: In this study, we analyzed a limited number (n = 3) of swimming trials using PIV.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample size for PIV analysis.

claim: The goal of PIV analysis was to investigate the underlying mechanism of vortex interactions following kinematic analysis that showed frequency and phase synchronization.
source: Our goal was to use these trials to investigate the underlying mechanism of vortex interactions following the kinematic analysis that showed both frequency and phase synchronization between fish and the flapping foil.
evidence: This is a statement about the purpose of the PIV analysis.

claim: Insight was gained on single and double-sided vortex interactions and on reduced pressure drag via computational inference.
source: We were able to gain insight on single and double-sided vortex interactions and on reduced pressure drag via computational inference.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the PIV and pressure analysis.

claim: There is expected to be a critical distance from the foil centerline at which fish transition from double to single-sided interactions.
source: We expect that there is a critical distance from the foil centerline at which fish transition from double to single-sided interactions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed patterns of vortex interaction.

claim: A larger sample size is required to identify and quantify the critical distance for transition between interaction types.
source: To further identify and quantify this critical distance a larger sample size is required.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future work.

claim: More swimming trials are required to quantify the reduction in pressure drag depending on the distance from the foil.
source: We will also require more swimming trials to quantify the reduction in pressure drag depending on the distance from the foil.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future work.

claim: Quantifying pressure drag reduction at different distances could help understand if and where there are distances that are optimal in terms of energy savings.
source: This could help to understand if and where there are distances that are optimal in terms of energy savings, as, e.g., suggested in Saadat et al., 2021.
evidence: This is speculation about potential insights from future work, with reference to prior literature.

claim: There are a number of hydrodynamically beneficial schooling positions known from past studies.
source: We know from past studies that there are a number of hydrodynamically beneficial schooling positions (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary of established knowledge from the literature.

claim: The results complement existing work with regard to fish swimming in thrust wakes shed by leading individuals during in-line locomotion.
source: Our results complement this body of work with regard to fish swimming in thrust wakes that are shed by leading individuals, a condition encountered within fish schools during in-line locomotion.
evidence: This is a statement about how the current work fits into the broader literature.

claim: The controlled experiments show that trout volitionally swim in thrust wakes and exhibit advantageous flow interactions with incoming vortices suggesting increased energy efficiency for in-line swimming.
source: In our controlled experiments, we show that trout volitionally swim in thrust wakes and exhibit advantageous flow interactions with incoming vortices suggesting increased energy efficiency for the in-line swimming condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The results highlight the hydrodynamic complexity of fish schooling.
source: These results highlight the hydrodynamic complexity of fish schooling and support a view in which individuals in schools have a variety of opportunities to save energy when they swim side-by-side, in drag wakes, and in thrust wakes behind each other.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Individuals in schools have a variety of opportunities to save energy when they swim side-by-side, in drag wakes, and in thrust wakes behind each other.
source: These results highlight the hydrodynamic complexity of fish schooling and support a view in which individuals in schools have a variety of opportunities to save energy when they swim side-by-side, in drag wakes, and in thrust wakes behind each other.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the current findings with prior knowledge about schooling.

claim: Particle image velocity trials were carried out for larger fish (n=3).
source: Particle image velocity trials were carried out for larger fish (n=3).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Trout were held at a water temperature of 16°C.
source: Trout were held at a water temperature of 16°C and all experiments were performed in accordance with Harvard animal care and use guidelines, IACUC protocol number 20-03-3 to GL.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions.

claim: All experiments were performed in accordance with Harvard animal care and use guidelines, IACUC protocol number 20-03-3.
source: Trout were held at a water temperature of 16°C and all experiments were performed in accordance with Harvard animal care and use guidelines, IACUC protocol number 20-03-3 to GL.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.
